opinions.rationale: Inverted-prior search did not find a routine selection criterion that jointly optimizes treatment prediction, longitudinal balance, weight dispersion, and an influence-function remainder for longitudinal nuisance models. SuperLearner (as used by ltmle and related stacks) still cross-validates predictive risk; CV-TMLE and related work improve targeting of the final parameter after nuisance fitting but do not replace predictive CV for the treatment, censoring, and outcome libraries themselves. Collaborative TMLE (C-TMLE) is the closest prior art: it selects confounder models using a targeted, collaborative criterion rather than pure prediction, and longitudinal/scalable C-TMLE variants exist. That is covariate-and-collaborative selection for TMLE, not a multi-metric SuperLearner loss for sustained-regime MSM, g-formula, g-estimation, or LTMLE libraries. Point-treatment work on balance-versus-discrimination for propensity scores (for example Diaz on balancing criteria) does not cover sequential longitudinal nuisance selection. Package surfaces checked in search (ltmle SuperLearner interface, SuperLearner defaults, SAS SUPERLEARNER 2024/2025) still select on predictive CV. No 2024 to 2026 AJE/Epidemiology/SiM-style paper or CRAN default library was found that implements the combined causal objective the problem names. Searches included: causal cross-validation SuperLearner longitudinal TMLE balance weight dispersion; causal loss OR targeted cross-validation nuisance MSM; collaborative TMLE longitudinal SuperLearner; propensity SuperLearner balance loss 2023 to 2026.

The claim that continuous-time dynamic-regime identification under irregular, process-driven observation is essentially without an identification theorem is stronger than the literature allows. Rytgaard, Gerds, and van der Laan (Annals of Statistics 2022) give a continuous-time counting-process TMLE for intervention-specific means when treatment, covariates, and outcomes occur at subject-specific times; intensities track monitoring; dynamic regimes on treatment assigned are defined with visit times kept as they naturally occur; and identification is via continuous-time g-computation under sequential exchangeability and positivity on the product-integral likelihood. Røysland, Ryalen, Nygård, and Didelez (JRSS-B 2025; arXiv:2202.02311) supply nonparametric graphical identification criteria for marginal effects of interventions on treatment-process intensities in continuous-time survival and event-history models, including structural conditions on censoring beyond classical independent censoring. Earlier continuous-time MSM and structural nested model work (Røysland; Ryalen et al. on prostate cancer) already stated filtration-based sequential exchangeability. What remains open, and why this is only partial: applied g-methods still default to discrete grids (Tankpinou et al. arXiv:2603.15924 still treats time partitioning as a consequential modeling choice); Rytgaard's main identification path intervenes on treatment decisions while leaving the visit intensity natural, so full dynamic control of a treatment-dependent informative visit process plus within-interval effects is not a closed applied recipe for EHR; software for continuous-time LTMLE is not yet a routine TTE default. Proposal papers that add unmeasured confounding (for example arXiv:2604.00544) are not resolutions. Identification theory exists; the residual gap is completeness for treatment-dependent observation, within-interval estimands, and routine practice.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: Continuous-time identification and efficient estimation results for dynamic interventions under counting-process filtrations and irregular monitoring exist (Rytgaard et al. 2022; Røysland et al. 2025), but they do not yet fully settle treatment-dependent informative visit processes with within-interval effects as a default applied apparatus, and most emulations still discretize time without an identification theorem tied to the chosen grid.

resolving_work.title: Continuous-time targeted minimum loss-based estimation of intervention-specific mean outcomes
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Provides continuous-time counting-process identification (g-computation on product integrals) and efficient TMLE for time-varying and dynamic treatment interventions when monitoring times are subject-specific; models monitoring intensities and covers dynamic regimes on treatment assigned with natural visit schedules.
resolving_work.quote: This paper generalizes the targeted minimum loss-based estimation (TMLE) framework to allow for estimating the effects of time-varying interventions in settings where both interventions, covariates, and the outcome can happen at subject-specific time-points on an arbitrarily fine time-scale.

resolving_work.title: Graphical criteria for the identification of marginal causal effects in continuous-time survival and event-history analyses
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: States nonparametric graphical identification criteria for marginal effects of interventions on continuous-time treatment-process intensities using local independence / counting-process graphs, including structural conditions on censoring; directly supplies the filtration-style identification theorem the agenda says is missing.
resolving_work.quote: To establish whether valid inference about the interventional situation can be drawn from typical observational, i.e. non-experimental, data we propose graphical rules indicating whether the observed information is sufficient to identify the desired causal effect by suitable re-weighting.

resolving_work.title: Time Partitioning in Target Trial Emulation
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Does not close identification; documents that discrete time partitioning remains a consequential open modeling choice in applied TTE, which supports residual openness after continuous-time theory.
resolving_work.quote: In target trial emulation, time partitioning enables researchers to handle time-varying confounders and immortal time bias with appropriate methods.

counter_evidence.quote: We consider a continuous-time counting process model where intensity measures track the monitoring of subjects, and focus on a low-dimensional target parameter defined as the intervention-specific mean outcome at the end of follow-up.
Our results establish general non-parametric identifiability and do not rely on particular survival models.

opinions.rationale: The core claim survives: after eligibility, active-comparator restriction, and inverse-probability weighting, information can collapse far below the nominal N, and papers still lead with headcount rather than information. What exists does not close the agenda item. Kish-style ESS, WeightIt::ESS, and cobalt balance tables already report weight-based effective sample size (including longitudinal MSM balance displays); Zhang, Bujkiewicz, and Jackson (BMC Medical Research Methodology 2024; 10.1186/s12874-024-02412-1) add three ESS estimators aimed at population-adjusted indirect comparison and general weighted analyses. Those are diagnostics for precision loss, not small-sample inference for estimated longitudinal weights plus outcome models, not time-varying ESS conventions for MSM/LTMLE follow-up, and not a simulation standard for when asymptotic intervals stop covering as a function of weight tails and event rates. lmtp's modified treatment policies help keep positivity usable but do not solve ESS reporting or finite-sample theory. No 2024 to 2026 reporting guideline (TARGET 2025, HARPER, STaRT-RWE, ENCePP) was found that requires ESS alongside nominal N at each follow-up time. Searches: effective sample size inverse probability weights MSM longitudinal 2024 2025; Zhang Bujkiewicz Jackson ESS; WeightIt ESS cobalt; small sample inference IPW MSM sandwich correction; TARGET ESS reporting. Vote open because the agenda's open parts (estimator-specific time-varying ESS convention, weight-aware small-sample theory, reporting incentive) remain; partial software and population-adjustment ESS papers are caveats, not solutions.

No estimator family is established as a default for longitudinal target-trial emulation of sustained strategies, and no current reporting or protocol standard requires a three-family comparison (weighting, outcome modeling, doubly robust) on the same data. Prior art that does not close the gap: (i) simulation comparisons of g-computation, IPTW/OW, and TMLE exist but are fragmented across data-generating mechanisms and often point-treatment or externally controlled trial settings (for example Schuler and Rose; Ren et al. 2023); (ii) software already makes multi-family analysis feasible (ltmle implements LTMLE, IPTW, and g-computation; lmtp implements sequential DR and related estimators; TrialEmulation covers sequence-of-trials ITT/PP), which lowers cost but does not create a requirement or a shared benchmark; (iii) TARGET 2025 (JAMA/BMJ) is a reporting guideline for target-trial emulations and does not mandate multi-estimator families; HARPER and STaRT-RWE structure protocols and sensitivity analyses without requiring weighting-plus-outcome-plus-DR comparison under a common estimand. No public continuous-time or informative-visit benchmark synthesizing the fragmented simulations was found. The problem's claim about incentives against multi-estimator reporting remains accurate. Searches: comparing IPTW g-formula TMLE longitudinal target trial multi-method 2024 2025; TARGET checklist multiple estimators; HARPER STaRT-RWE sensitivity g-methods; Schuler Rose TMLE IPW g-computation.
